title: The Righteous
hook: non-Jews who risked their lives to hide and save Jews
carry: someone knocked, you open the door

segments.voice: Yesterday, mered, the revolt, and your line: they fought. Today, courage of another kind, from people on the other side of the walls.

A tree on a hillside in Jerusalem, with a small plaque at its foot. On the plaque, a name that isn't Jewish: a farmer's, perhaps, or a nun's, or a diplomat's. Walk a little further and there's another tree, another name. Each marks someone who was not Jewish, who lived through the Nazi years, and who hid a Jewish neighbor in an attic, forged a paper, or opened a door when opening it could have cost everything. Some were caught. Some were never thanked in their lifetimes. Today, the title they were given.
screen: `A TREE ON A HILLSIDE.` → `A NAME THAT ISN'T JEWISH.` → `A DOOR THAT COULD COST EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial, gives these people a title: Righteous Among the Nations. In Hebrew, chasidei umot ha-olam. The idea is much older than the war. A rabbinic teaching in the Tosefta says the righteous of the nations of the world have a share in the world to come. Goodness, in that teaching, doesn't belong to one people. The stories are as different as the people. André and Magda Trocmé, a pastor and his wife in the French village of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, where villagers took in Jewish children and refugees. Chiune Sugihara, a Japanese diplomat in Lithuania, who kept writing transit visas after his government had said no. Irena Sendler, a social worker in Warsaw, who helped smuggle children out of the ghetto. And people whose names are known only to the families they hid, or to no one at all. Asked later why they did it, some rescuers gave answers so plain they sound almost like a shrug. Someone knocked. You open the door. The book of Proverbs asks the same of its reader: rescue those being dragged toward death, and don't hold back. No one, it adds, can excuse themselves by saying they didn't know. Remembering the righteous doesn't soften the history around them. It shows something harder: even then, a person could still choose.
screen: `RIGHTEOUS AMONG THE NATIONS.` · `A VILLAGE, A DIPLOMAT, A SOCIAL WORKER.` · `SOMEONE KNOCKED. YOU OPEN THE DOOR.` · `RESCUE THOSE DRAGGED TOWARD DEATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who once took a risk on your behalf, and small counts: a teacher who stood up for you, a friend who told you a hard truth, a stranger who stopped when others walked past. Let their face come clear, and notice what the risk might have cost them. If you pray, give thanks for them in the words of your own tradition; if not, simply hold them in mind with gratitude.
The Righteous. In full, the Righteous Among the Nations: people who were not Jewish and risked their lives to hide and save Jews.
Your line: someone knocked, you open the door. A plain answer, and a life behind it. Day one thousand seventeen.

howItsDone: Jewish communities honor rescuers through Yad Vashem's title Righteous Among the Nations, with trees and names at the memorial in Jerusalem; some families stay in touch with the families of those who hid them.

chat.says: Why does a Holocaust memorial honor people who weren't Jewish?
options: They risked their lives to save Jews, and goodness isn't one people's.
They were honored for converting to Judaism once the war ended.
It's mainly a thank-you to the Allied armies that won the war.

notes: Audit: the hook said every honoree 'lived under Nazi rule', which does not fit Chiune Sugihara (consul in Kaunas, Lithuania, 1940, not under German occupation); now 'lived through the Nazi years'. The practice and carry (thank someone who took a risk for you) sit close to day 1016's carry (name one person's courage to them); kept because the outline sets the practice, but a Keeper may want a different carry task.
Claims rule: no numbers of rescuers or of trees are given. The trees on the Avenue/Garden of the Righteous at Yad Vashem are described only as 'a tree on a hillside'.

Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2: printed editions read tzaddikei (righteous) umot ha-olam; the Yad Vashem title uses chasidei umot ha-olam. The script says 'the idea' is older, not the exact Hebrew title. Please check the wording and the original-game spelling.

The Yad Vashem medal inscription ('whoever saves a single life saves an entire universe') is described as a line from the Mishnah; note that manuscripts of Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 differ on 'a single life' vs 'a single life of Israel'. Please confirm the paraphrase is fair.
Rescuer examples (the Trocmés and Le Chambon; Sugihara in Kaunas; Irena Sendler in Warsaw) are stated briefly; all three are recognized by Yad Vashem. Please check.
'Some of them were caught' is general; a Keeper may want a named example or to cut it.
